messages.subject: morphol.disparity bootstrap
parts:
Is there a way to generate a 95% confidence interval for the calculation of procrustes variance within each group? I've tried editing the morphol.disparity function, but it's proven particularly difficult when trying to incorporate phylogeny, as I don't necessarily want to bootstrap the PGLS as well. 

Thanks in advance for any advice you can offer!

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] morphol.disparity bootstrap
parts:
Sarah,

I recommend that instead of using morphol.disparity - which just uses the residuals from a procD.lm object, perhaps generated from procD.pgls - you use the procD.lm object created by procD.pgls and create a bootstrap procedure directly from it.  You can create a for loop where in every iteration, you either resample the data (by rows) with replacement and re-obtain a PGLS result (procD.pgls with iter = 1), or my preference, you resample residuals (not pgls.residuals) with replacement (again by rows), add these to fitted values (not pgls.fitted values), re-obtain a pgls result (iter = 1) and then get a morphol.disparity result for 1 iteration.  Doing one of these for every bootstrap iteration will create distributions of bootstrapped Procrustes variances from which confidence intervals can be estimated, holding the phylogenetic correction constant (not randomizing it).  (The latter approach also holds model effects, if any, constant.)

My suggestion assumes you are comfortable with using for loops (or maybe vectorization with apply-like functions) and extracting attributes from procD.lm objects.  I’ll gladly provide more detail if needed, but chose not to get too technical for this forum response.  Let me know if you want a direct email with an example.

Most of our functions use randomization of residuals rather than bootstrapping.  Regarding the bootstrapping, there are philosophically diverse methods (as my example above illustrates).  This makes it hard to include something like this in our hypothesis testing functions.  Furthermore, the random pairwise differences in Procrustes distance you can extract are similar to generating confidence intervals for the differences between variances, which is more in line with two-sample hypothesis tests.

Hope that helps in some way!

Mike
